Recently I posted a query regarding estimating the probability of =
detection for distances <w. Below I provide a summary of my results =
based on suggestions from others and my own investigation.

In my original email I didn't clearly explain that what I wanted was the =
probability of detection for distances <w (i.e., the area under the =
detection curve for some distance x, where x<w), not just the detection =
probability at distance x.

Why would one want to do this? In my case, many people survey grassland =
birds using strip transects and assume the probability of detection is =
1.0. And the strip widths used vary greatly. I wanted to use my data =
to estimate probabilities of detection at various strip widths.

It is possible to obtain the probability of detection for x<w, as well =
as a 95% CI, using Distance, but only for simple detection functions. =
First, you analyze your data and select the best model (it can only be a =
half-normal with no adjustments or a uniform with a 2nd-order =
adjustment). Second, re-run the analysis with the bootstrap variance =
(and bootstrap output file) but only permit the model you selected to be =
estimated in all the bootstrap runs.

The third step gets more involved and depends on the model function.

1. From the bootstrap output you can obtain f(0) and the transect width =
(w) for each resample.
2. Using (1) you can obtain the parameter estimate for each resample. =
For the uniform with a 2nd-order adjustment solve for A(1) from the =
following relationship:
f(0) =3D 1/[(1+A(1)/3)*w]
where w is the width for the resample.

For the half-normal you have to iteratively solve the following equation

f(0) =3D 1/sqrt(2*pi)*A(1)*[PHI(w(i)/A(1)-.5)] =
where pi=3D3.14159265, PHI() is the cdf for the normal distribution, =
sqrt() is the square root, and w(i) is the width of interest, i.e., =
w(i)<w.

3. After solving for A(1) for each resample you can calculate the =
probability of detection over the interval 0 to w(i) for the uniform w/ =
2nd-order adj as

P(from 0 to w(i)) =3D =
(w(i)/w+A(1)/w**3/3*w(i)**3)/(w(i)/w)

and for the half-normal as

P(from 0 to w(i)) =
=3D(SQRT(2*pi)*A(1)*(PHI(w(i)/A(1))-0.5))/w(i)

Fourth, now that you have the probability of detection for each =
resample, simply select the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles to obtain a 95% CI =
(note: the point estimate is obtained by plugging in the coefficient =
values from the Distance output into (3)).


The reason you can only obtain these values for the simplest uniform and =
half-normal functions is that all other functions have >1 coefficient =
(even the simplest hazard function) and you end up with 1 equation with =
> >2 unknown coefficients. What is needed are the coefficients for each =
resample run, but that is not currently available in the bootstrap =
output in Distance. That way you would simply plug in the coefficients =
and could either analytically or iteratively estimate the area under the =
detection function for the width of interest.

Another possibility is to integrate the model function and then use the =
delta method to estimate a variance and obtain CIs, but I suspect the =
bootstrap is still a much better approach, and my calculus is too rusty =
to integrate the hazard function (if it's even possible)! If someone =
out there can integrate the hazard, please let me know!

Thanks to Jeff Laake and Steve Buckland for their help and suggestions =
(but all the errors are my own!).

Duane
